title: Hyderabad Police Seize 25,000 Kg of Adulterated Spices Laced With Industrial Dyes
excerpt: Raids on 13 spice processing units uncover fabric dye, synthetic colours, and talcum powder being used to make low-quality spices appear premium, part of a 140-day crackdown that has seized 246 tonnes of suspect food products.
body:
• Hyderabad police and food safety officials raided 13 spice processing units, seizing 25,000 kg of spices adulterated with industrial dyes, cloth dyes, and talcum powder.
  • The raids are part of a 140-day crackdown that has resulted in 659 enforcement operations, 202 FIRs, and seizure of nearly 246 tonnes of suspected adulterated food products.
  • Investigators found fabric dye and synthetic colours being used on cloves, shahjeera, and ajwain to make them appear premium-grade for higher prices.
  • Three people were arrested in connection with the spice adulteration cases, with further action expected based on ongoing investigations.

Industrial Dyes Found in Everyday Spices

Hyderabad police and food safety officials have seized approximately 25,000 kg of spices from 13 processing and trading establishments across the city after raids uncovered the widespread use of industrial dyes, synthetic colours, and other harmful substances to adulterate common kitchen staples.

The H-FAST team of the Hyderabad Commissioner's Task Force, working alongside GHMC Food Safety officials, found that operators were using synthetic orange, red, and green food colours, permanent industrial dyes, cloth dyes, talcum powder, and rice-bran oil to enhance the appearance, shine, weight, and volume of spices before selling them at inflated prices.

At one facility, investigators discovered that low-quality and rejected mustard stocks were being mixed with fabric dye, talcum powder, and oil to artificially boost their appearance and weight. At other units, premium spices including cloves and shahjeera were coated with synthetic colours to mimic a brighter, higher-grade product. Permanent industrial dyes — substances never intended for human consumption — were found in shahjeera, ajwain, and other essential spices.

Part of a Wider 140-Day Crackdown

The spice seizures are the latest action in H-FAST's broader food adulteration campaign, which has now run for 140 days. Over that period, officials have conducted 659 enforcement operations, registered 202 first information reports, and seized nearly 246 tonnes of suspected adulterated or contaminated food products. Another 232 cases have been referred to food safety officers for statutory action.

The crackdown's scope extends well beyond spices. Officials inspected 83 ghee outlets and 46 paneer outlets, while 96 online public complaints were addressed. Among the most alarming discoveries: more than 27,000 kg of ginger-garlic paste allegedly prepared using unpeeled or rotten ingredients and chemicals including titanium dioxide and acetic acid. Investigators also found more than 12 tonnes of rotten meat and 60 tonnes of chicken waste stored in unhygienic conditions.

"We will continue strict enforcement against food adulteration and activities that pose a threat to public health. The safety of citizens remains our priority, and those violating food safety norms will face legal action."

— VC Sajjanar, Commissioner of Police, Hyderabad City

Three Arrested, More Action Expected

The operation resulted in cases being registered at Mailardevpally and Balapur police stations. Three individuals — Rahul Bhati, Vishal Panwar, and Dulichand Kachhawar — were arrested in connection with the adulteration. Police and food safety officials indicated that enforcement operations would continue across Hyderabad based on credible information and public complaints.

The arrests highlight an enforcement model that combines policing muscle with food safety expertise. The H-FAST unit, established specifically for food-related crime, has the authority to conduct raids, make arrests, and register criminal cases — a more aggressive approach than traditional food safety inspections, which often result in notices and fines rather than criminal prosecution.

A Recurring Challenge for India's Spice Industry

India is the world's largest producer, consumer, and exporter of spices, an industry valued at over $10 billion annually. But food adulteration remains a persistent problem, driven by thin margins, weak enforcement, and a fragmented supply chain dominated by small-scale processors and traders.

The Hyderabad crackdown follows a 2024 scandal involving major Indian spice brands whose products were found to contain elevated levels of ethylene oxide, leading to recalls in Hong Kong, Singapore, and other markets. That episode prompted calls for stricter testing protocols and greater regulatory oversight across the spice supply chain.

For the Indian diaspora, the implications extend beyond domestic food safety. Indian spices are widely exported and sold in grocery stores from London to Toronto to Sydney. While established export brands face international quality checks, smaller operators and informal supply chains remain less regulated, raising questions about what reaches consumers at home and abroad.
